newsitem.title: CANADA: Berkley CEO says big gains to continue.
newsitem.headline: Berkley CEO says big gains to continue.

text.p: Berkley Petroleum Corp, whose stock price more than doubled in the last year as it made big oil and gas discoveries, should keep pumping out major financial and production gains, Chief Executive Michael Rose said on Tuesday.
Berkley, which made waves in 1996 with its Midale oil discovery in southeast Saskatchewan, was expected to post 1997 cash flow of C$70 million or C$4.24 a share, Rose told the Berkley annual meeting.
That would be up from C$26.2 million or C$1.84 a share in 1996.
Earnings for this year were projected at about C$20 million or C$1.21 a share, up from C$10.8 million or C$0.75 a share last year.
Rose said the financial forecasts were based on assumptions of a C$1.60 per thousand cubic feet natural gas price and a C$24 per barrel crude oil price.
Production was on track to average 15,000 barrels of oil equivalent a day in 1996 and exit the year at 20,000 barrels a day, he said.
Last year, the company's output averaged 6,000 BOED.
Production was expected to hit 30,000 BOED sometime in 1998, Rose said.
At the meeting, shareholders approved a three-for-one split of the company's red-hot shares, which was expected to occur in 10 business days.

Rose outlined numerous exploration and production plays the company was targeting in western Alberta, northeastern British Columbia and the Northwest Territories to show it was more than a one-hit wonder.
Capital spending for the year was budgeted at C$135 million, up from C$68 million last year.

"The nature of the exploration business is you don't know which one is going to work," he told reporters after the meeting. "To me, the smartest strategy is to be in a number of different exploration venues and then see what happens."
The company expected to participate in 40 new pool wildcat wells in 1997, up from an orginal budget of 20, Rose said.

In northeast British Columbia., where the company has operations near Fort St. John, gas production was expected to hit 75 million cubic feet a day at the end of 1997, a dramatic jump from Berkley's 30 million cubic feet a day 1996 exit rate, he said.
It was also expected to test the region's Doig geological zone oil potential with a well later this year.
The Doig is the formation that has propelled Remington Energy's recent oil production growth.
At Carstairs-Crossfield in central Alberta, where Elkton production had been shut in over the winter, output was on track to meet or beat 30 million cubic feet a day, he said.

Meanwhile, Berkley continues to drill to test possible extensions of the Midale Red River Ordovician oil play in Saskatchewan and expects to drill six to seven wildcats there before the end of this year.

"Twenty-five development wells have been drilled so far, so I think we understand the size of the original Midale accumulation," Rose said. "The question now is, are there more of them out there and that's what a number of oil and gas companies are pursuing right now in that part of the world."
He also said Berkley had yet to test numerous uphole zones at Midale.
Berkley shares climbed 1.60 to 38.50 in Toronto on Tuesday. The stock has climbed from 17.75 a year ago.
((Reuters Calgary Bureau (403) 531-1624))
